---
title: "Why marriage?"
description: "A personal essay on what marriage is for, and why I have chosen not to marry."
author: "Maedbh King"
---

Part of [Married, or not](index.qmd). This page is my own view. The rest of the project sticks to the law and the numbers.

The figures speak for themselves. According to the CSO's Census 2022, the number of cohabiting couples without children grew more than twice as fast as the number of married couples without children between 2016 and 2022: up 20%, against 8%.^[CSO, Census 2022, table [F3035](https://data.cso.ie/table/F3035): cohabiting couples without children rose from 76,715 to 91,694, and married couples without children from 278,934 to 302,358.] Today, about one in six Irish couples cohabit.^[176,956 of 1,059,955 couples in Census 2022, CSO table [F3035](https://data.cso.ie/table/F3035).] There were 3.8 marriages for every 1,000 people in 2024, down from 4.0 the year before.^[CSO, [Marriages 2024](https://www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/ep/p-mar/marriages2024/mainresults/).] These are not the numbers of a society that enthusiastically endorses marriage. They are the numbers of a society quietly voting with its feet.

The question we ought to be asking, but rarely do in polite Irish company, is whether women, in particular, have good reason to be sceptical.

To ask what marriage is *for* is already to begin unsettling it. The philosopher Clare Chambers has argued that marriage as a state institution bundles together an arbitrary collection of human goods (love, commitment, sexual fidelity, financial interdependence, procreation) and rewards only those who organise their lives in one particular, legally recognised way.^[Clare Chambers, *Against Marriage: An Egalitarian Defence of the Marriage-Free State* (Oxford University Press, 2017).] Why should the State privilege this configuration above all others? The answer, historically, has had less to do with love than with property, inheritance, and the control of women's bodies and labour.

John Stuart Mill, writing in *The Subjection of Women* in 1869, did not mince his words: the legal subordination of women was "the primitive state of slavery lasting on".^[J. S. Mill, *The Subjection of Women* (1869), chapter 1. [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/27083/27083-h/27083-h.htm).] Simone de Beauvoir observed that for women, marriage was historically the only socially permissible route to sexual experience and motherhood: not a free choice, but the only alternative to punishment and exclusion. Kate Millett, in *Sexual Politics*, wrote that "Patriarchy's chief institution is the family", the mechanism by which the subordination of women is reproduced across generations.^[Kate Millett, *Sexual Politics* (1970), chapter 2. [Marxists Internet Archive](https://www.marxists.org/subject/women/authors/millett-kate/theory.htm).]

Marriage has played a significant role in maintaining the wider regime of gender inequality. It has been used, historically, to consolidate legal, economic, cultural, and symbolic oppression, confining women to a private sphere in which they were, and in many respects remain, seriously disadvantaged.

The radical feminist Sheila Cronan pointed out that the marriage contract is the only important legal contract whose terms are never written down. Wives have long been expected to perform an enormous and economically invisible quantity of domestic and caring labour: in Cronan's account, a full-time job without pay. In Ireland, this was not merely a cultural expectation but a constitutional one.

Article 41.2 of Bunreacht na hÉireann, adopted in 1937 and drafted under the heavy influence of Catholic social teaching, declares that "by her life within the home, woman gives to the State a support without which the common good cannot be achieved", and commits the State to "endeavour to ensure that mothers shall not be obliged by economic necessity to engage in labour to the neglect of their duties in the home".^[As quoted by the [Electoral Commission](https://www.electoralcommission.ie/referendum/referendums-on-family-and-care/).] When the people were finally asked in March 2024 to replace this language, they said no, for complicated reasons.^[[Electoral Commission](https://www.electoralcommission.ie/referendum/referendums-on-family-and-care/): "The proposal was rejected by the people."] The language remains. In 2026, the Irish Constitution still embeds a vision of married women as the unpaid custodians of domestic life. I reject that categorisation.

The history of divorce in this country is equally instructive. Ireland's Constitution prohibited divorce until 1996. A first referendum to remove the ban, in 1986, failed by 63.5% to 36.5%. When divorce was finally approved in 1995, it passed by just over 9,000 votes: 50.28% to 49.72%.^[1986: 538,279 for and 935,843 against; 1995: 818,842 for and 809,728 against. [Tenth Amendment of the Constitution Bill 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenth_Amendment_of_the_Constitution_Bill_1986); [Fifteenth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifteenth_Amendment_of_the_Constitution_of_Ireland).] The State's very architecture presumed the permanence of marriage, with no exit for women trapped in unhappy or abusive unions. The feminist philosopher Claudia Card drew out the implication: without marriage, a woman can take her life back without meeting the law as an obstacle. With marriage, and without divorce, Irish women had no such option.

It is sometimes argued that liberal democracies have now abolished the explicit legal inequalities of marriage (equal property rights, access to divorce, no marriage bar) and that the feminist critique of the institution has therefore lost its force. This argument is too comfortable. The feminist case against marriage today operates on two levels: the practical and the symbolic.

At the practical level, marriage continues to shape material life in ways that disproportionately disadvantage women. Unpaid care and domestic work, while not legally compelled, remains overwhelmingly feminised within marriage. Women who reduce their working hours or leave the workforce to raise children suffer lasting earnings penalties, pension deficits, and dependency. The "marriage bonus" that economists identify largely accrues to men; the "marriage penalty", in terms of career and earning power, largely falls on women.

At the symbolic level, marriage continues to function as a norm: a template against which other forms of life are measured and found wanting. It encodes a particular vision of gender, sexuality, and domesticity as natural and inevitable. To refuse it is still, in many quarters, to invite suspicion or pity.

None of this means that individual marriages cannot be loving, egalitarian, and freely chosen. Many are. But the institution is not reducible to its best instances. As Clare Chambers reminds us, the question is not whether some couples flourish within marriage, but whether the State should continue to single out this one configuration of human intimacy for special legal recognition, and whether women, in particular, are well served by continuing to do so.

The rising tide of cohabitation in Ireland suggests that growing numbers of women have already arrived at their own answer. It is time our public conversation caught up.
